Its an intense practice match against a local university team. Our club was already ahead slightly and our outside just slammed the ball on a clean side out.
I rotate to position 1, it was my turn to serve. I wasn't exactly feeling confident today, but the ball seemed to fit my hand nicely while hitting against the wall.
I take my usual 6 steps back from the service line, breathing in and out slowly to control my performance anxiety which I always faced playing against other teams.
I do my routine, and toss the ball high. It felt just right and I jump. Still holding back slightly from being scared of missing on my first serve, I hit the ball with around 70% of my strength. A loud slap signifies a perfect contact and the ball dips hard just before it reaches their left receiver. It was an ace, but not a satisfying one.
The ball comes back, and I go for another. With more confidence in my steps, I did my routine exactly the same, and the toss was slightly lower than usual. Risking it for the biscuit, I put everything into the hit and contacted it slightly to the right, adding a tiny bit of spin that curved the ball right between position 1 and 6. They fumble and the ball ricochets off their hands and far behind them.
I went again, but this time the toss was way too forward. I jump horizontally into the court as much as I can and prayed I didnt step on the line, pushing the ball lightly and rolling it between the middle and opposite not partaking in the serve receive. They panic and they go out of system, forcing them to push it high over to their outside. A monster block by our middle allows me to go again.
Three more rips and three service aces later I was exhausted. Thats 6 points in a row and 3 aces in a row. My heart was pumping and the adrenaline was flowing through my blood.
Using the remaining strength I had, I tossed the ball high and into the court, forcing myself to reach for it and I barely managed to. With a full swing the ball flew higher than I thought, but was going incredibly fast. Everyone expected it to fly out, but it dips perfectly into the edge of the end line and that marks my 6th service ace in a row. I roared with my ego boosted beyond belief and my team cheered with me. It felt amazing. I havent made any plays like this in months and it revived a part of me.
Then I got too tired, did a standing float and their opposite crushes the ball on a sideout.
Worth.
(Source: The very match I had hours ago)

TL;DR: I'm looking for a shoe that is lightweight, with minimal cushioning.
https://www.reddit.com/r/volleyball/comments/707q5r/do_volleyball_shoes_make_a_difference/
I'm drawing inspiration from u/JavierTheNormal in his comment. He/she says that oftentimes, we can't sacrifice the cushioning of a shoe to minimize heel impact for the weight of the shoe.
My Experience: I can't jump well with heavy shoes. I prefer lightweight shoes that I can slip on with a nice pair of elastic laces because it feels natural. I'm also part of the barefoot running community (although I haven't run barefoot), but i like the concept of "natural running". So, I've been looking on reddits and websites to see WHY we need cushioning. Obviously to prevent injuries. I have limited experience with playing actual volleyball games, but I'm looking to play seriously. So, I probably dont understand the importance of cushioning since I havent had to jump as much as y'all.
I'm wondering because I've been in store to try on some asics and the cushioning, which asics is known for, is a bit too much from my perspective. It feels heavy when I try to jump. I know there's also traction that has to be factored in, which is super important in lateral movement, agility, etc.
If the conventional volleyball shoe is good bc it cushions the landing, but it wont allow you to reach higher heights bc of the cushioning, should I just say fuck it and opt for a lighter option?
Can y'all recommend me a lightweight shoe with minimal cushioning or is it a shot in the dark?

Hi, I’m new to Reddit—this is my first post.
I’d love to hear about your child’s developmental milestones in volleyball, or if you’re a player yourself, how your skills progressed when you were starting out.
I have a 13-year-old daughter. She’s on the taller side for her age, and she only started playing volleyball in mid-March (about 1.5 months ago). So far, she’s had:
• 19 private lessons (2 hours each, usually with just 1–2 other kids)
• She also goes to the court 3–4 times a week to practice on her own for 1–2 hours
Here are some of the things she can already do:
On her own:
• Wall drills: can sustain about 50–70 controlled forearm passes
• Wall drills with variation: alternating higher and lower passes for around 20–30 reps
• Toss-to-pass drills off the wall (self-toss, then controlled receive, ~20–30 reps)
• Keeps the ball in play with continuous digging control, mixing lower and higher contacts
• Basic float serve: can get the ball over the net around 70% of the time, though it still lacks speed and power
With a partner:
• Can rally using forearm passes over a standard-height net with decent control
She hasn’t had any scrimmage or actual game experience yet, but she’s starting a volleyball camp next week where we’re hoping she’ll get that exposure.
Okay, here’s where I could use some advice. Over the past few sessions, her coach has been teaching her how to spike. But no matter how it’s explained or demonstrated, she’s really struggling to put the full movement together. Her arm swing and footwork don’t seem to sync up.
She’s had about 5 sessions focused on spiking so far. The coach keeps revisiting it each time, but the same mistakes keep happening. Even when it’s demonstrated clearly, she has a hard time translating that into her own movement.
Is this normal at this stage?
To be honest, I’ve always been a bit uncoordinated in sports, while my husband was a serious athlete in college. I can’t help but wonder if she takes after me in that area—and whether this is something she’ll eventually grow into.
My questions:
1. I know it’s still early, but realistically, how long does it take to learn proper spiking technique? How long did it take you or your child?
2. Can you share your (or your child’s) development timeline in volleyball—what skills came at what stage, and after how many months or years?
P.S. Just to add some context—she’s an overachiever and really wanted to use her summer break to focus on improving in volleyball. Her goal is to become team captain next year. It surprised me a bit given how new she is to the sport, but at the same time, she’s always been the type to set big goals and work toward them.
I try to help her break things down into steps and remind her that progress takes time and consistency—especially since many of the other girls trying out have already been playing for a year or two. She’s naturally a strong leader, but of course, skill level matters too when it comes to earning that role.

I don’t know what the situation is outside Italy, but here we have really bad sports news. Of course, soccer dominates the scene in an almost dictatorial way, but that’s not even the worst part. Soccer news, in fact, rarely cover topics such as game or team analysis, focusing instead on the latest tweet of player X or the latest Instagram pic of player Y’s wife that “drove the internet crazy”. In this depressing environment, there have been a couple of exceptions. The most prominent one is “[l’Ultimo Uomo](https://www.ultimouomo.com/)” (literally “the Last Man”), a sports website clearly inspired by now-defunct Grantland. Soccer is the dominant topic there as well, but their posts are interesting analysis of games, squads and players or tales about the past. Also, there’s an entire section dedicated to NBA basketball and another one to various sports. Volleyball is rarely covered, but there’s a very competent writer named Gian Marco Porcellini who is a pleasure to read when he writes about volleyball. His[ latest post](https://www.ultimouomo.com/wilfredo-leon-nuova-pallavolo/) is about how Wilfredo Leòn is changing volleyball. It’s a deep technical analysis of his game and I thought many people here would be interested, so I contacted the author and he gave me permission to translate some of his work here. I’ll skip most of the statistical analysis because I covered it many times in my posts, so I’ll focus on the more technical paragraphs. Beware, it’s a VERY LONG article for today’s standards (my translation is about 1,600 words long) but, hey, there’s a reason why they like Grantland! I just hope that, since they’ve been recently bought by Sky Sports, they won’t do to l’Ultimo Uomo what ESPN did to Grantland.
SPIKING
Leòn is 201 cm tall (6’ 7”) and can spike as high as 385 cm (12’ 7”), only Kaziyski (12’ 9”) can do better in Superleague. What makes him unique is his ability to avoid the block, despite using only a finite set of solutions and despite attacking in a relatively intricate and slow manner.
The quality of the pass, the speed of the set, the attacking zone, the run-up. None of those things matter. Almost 6 times out of 10 he will kill it, often with a cut shot that goes over the block or by its side. The blockers don’t matter either, because Leòn can tighten the cut even against 3 men and kill it in front row, with powerful and precise balls that no one can dig.
Thanks in part to De Cecco, Leòn is often able to fully extend his arm and hit the ball neatly at its highest point, creating trajectories that even the spectators can’t follow. Also, the very few times in which he goes for a lob or a whiff, the ball is hard to dig as well, because the back row is expecting the ball to go long and stays at the edge of the court.
With faster sets, closer to the antenna, Leòn prefers to hit on 6-5, mainly to anticipate the block, but he doesn’t need second tempos to avoid the block. In fact, in order to jump higher, charge the extra shoulder rotation and having more options available, he seems to prefer more arched balls, closer to third tempos.
In situations like those, the block should have an extra fraction of a second to position and invade. Leòn, instead, exploits those situations to float in the air, delaying the spike and offsetting the block timing. It’s like he and his opponents are part of the same video, but with different speeds.
Modern volleyball is getting faster and faster, with powerful hitters who try to anticipate the spike to outpace the block-defense. Still, Leòn is so dominant on a physical level that he almost seems to go on the opposite direction, slowing down until the very last moment. He loves the cut shot, but he can opt for a line shot when he’s 1 on 1, the setter is on front row or the block allows it.
While everyone is focused on Leòn’s huge athletic talent, we have to acknowledge his volleyball IQ as well. One of the reasons he’s so efficient on cut shots, in fact, is that he has great dexterity and kinesthesia, which allow him to target unguarded spots. In fact, among Superleague spikers, Leòn has the lowest attack error ratio, just 10.6% and well above Juantorena’s 11.9%.
Despite his spikes being (theoretically) predictable, it’s hard to read Leòn, also because his run-up doesn’t change significantly when he’s preparing either a cut or a line shot. For example, when he’s in 5 and doesn’t receive, he goes a few inches left outside the field, ending the run-up with the left foot, which is barely inside the ground the moment he jumps. It’s not the feet movement that directs the spike, but his instead his pelvis rotation.
Leòn is efficient not only from 4, but also on bics and pipes, a solution that De Cecco chooses often on counter attack. Leòn prefers the extra rotation when on front row, but on back row he tends to opt for direct 6-to-1 spikes. Lately, he’s been very efficient from 5 as well, in order to help Perugia escape P1, a solution that is rarely used in modern men’s volleyball.
SERVING
His deadly service is executed in an almost robot-like sequence. Leòn always starts from 1, about a meter inside the court, and hits along the run-up. Every other aspect is a constant. The jump height, the ball toss, the leap that allows him to hit at the apex and almost inside the 7-8 meters, and the jolt that “wraps” the ball, keeping the arm well extended for maximum power.
Usually, Leòn targets the middle of the ground and rarely looks for the lines. This means that, other than looking for the receivers’ overlap zones, he basically doesn’t change the arm’s rotation degree. Sometimes, when he’s on a series, he may choose to target a different receiver.
Most servers possess a wider set of choices than Leòn, making them less predictable but also increasing the error ratio, since an out-of-run service aimed at the lines does not follow the natural biomechanics and lowers both power and precision. As for his spikes, Leòn always follows a very precise pattern, probably due to an almost obsessive training ([here](https://youtu.be/mR961CtSiY0?t=192) you can watch him serve with a GoPro mounted on his head).
Among his many aces, there’s one that got stuck in my mind. On November 11th, against Modena, Leòn had just scored an ace with an incredibly powerful and precise ball that hit the ground just left of Urnaut. On the next serve, he threw a meteorite that equaled Zaytsev’s speed record (134 km/h), once again on the Slovenian OH who got hit in the chest. It almost looked like Urnaut didn’t even think about receiving that ball, but instead used his chest to protect himself, pretty much like when Wile E. Coyote opens the umbrella to shelter himself from that giant boulder.
Since his arrival in Superleague, Leòn has kept an insane ace ratio, much higher than in the past. In the last 4 Champions League seasons, he averaged 2.73 aces/match. He ended this season with 3.76. Also, he doesn’t miss much, 143 errors and 94 aces for -0.12 efficiency and a 1:1,52 ratio. His Italian Superleague record is 7 aces against Monza, while in last year’s Russian Superleague playoffs he got 10 against Kemerovo.
OTHER FUNDAMENTALS
It may look odd that such an excellent players in those fundamentals is so below average in the others. Still, volleyball underwent through a very high specialization in the last years. All-around players like Ngapeth or Kovacevic are the exception, not the rule. That said, it’s a pity that such a physical player is so weak on blocking, especially on reading, delaying the jump and helping the middle.
Leòn is 27th for blocks/set among Superleague spikers, with a 0.20 average. His OH buddy, Lanza, who doesn’t have neither the body nor the technique of an élite blocker, averages 0.25. In reception (16.7% perfect, 5% efficiency), he has problems dampening the ball with his legs and directing the pass. Also, when he has to flatten down, he tends to lose balance and kneel instead of keeping steady and land on the side.
He faces the same problems on defense, where he’s pretty bad on covering the space behind the block but at least average in position defense, in which he tries to get hit on his upper torso. The 2nd touch is way below average as well, since he often opts for a very predictable bump set without any creativity.
PERUGIA
In order to make room for Leòn, both on budget and on the lineup, Perugia let Zaytsev and Russell go, signing Lanza instead. The former Trento captain inherited the Tsar’s burden and he has to cover a lot of ground on reception, given Leòn’s poor mobility. Lanza had ups and downs this season, with decent numbers on offense (48,8% kills, but only 381 spikes. Leòn had 573, Atanasjevic 638), not so much on reception (20.6% perfect, 11% efficiency). His numbers are way worse than Zaytsev’s and even worse than Russell’s (21.8% perfect, 12% efficiency), who was the “offensive” OH. Those numbers should not be a surprise, however. Lanza and Colaci represent 2/3 of the Italian NT back row, who suffered a lot on reception and defense in the last WC against tough opponents.
Perugia looks like a bigger-scale Leòn, with ridiculously high kill % and ace ratio, but way below average reception (and blocking, if I may add). Its fortunes depend largely on him and Atanasjevic, who, in terms of highs and options width, is now the best OPP in the world along with Sokolov. The Cuban and the Serbian, together, score 56.2% of Perugia’s points and represent 60.0% of its spikes.
If the consecutive Atanasjevic-Leòn service turn doesn’t break havoc or one of them is below par, it gets very hard for Perugia to win. Perugia lost 3 times this season (against Padova, Monza and Trento). In all of these games, Atanasjevic never went over 45.8% kills, while Leòn had 48.3%, which is decent but way below his par, especially when his team has so little alternatives on high ball.
Aside from the difficulties in organizing the right spacing between blocking and defense, Bernardi often complained about how the flow gets interrupted when the sideout phase doesn’t work. After the win against Ravenna in December, he talked about “frequent, almost constant amnesia that can be very dangerous”. After the 3-0 defeat against Trento, first and (so far) only defeat against a top team this season, he said that “we’re having a hard time dealing with mistakes or good plays by our opponents, we’re a bit fragile”. Finally, after the tie-break win against Verona, he urged his players to “fill in the gaps”.
There’s an upside to all this, though. Perugia can afford to be less structured than other teams, to play a predictable volleyball and to be less effective on sideout, because they can rely on two excellent attackers and on a setter like De Cecco, who can turn any dumpster ball into an easy kill for the spiker. Perugia is the 2nd best team for break points and the worst for sideout points, and that says a lot.

I’ve been seeing a lot of posts on here asking for advice on how to jump serve. I’ve also been teaching a lot recently and have noticed some trends among new players learning to serve. I thought I’d share some insights and advice that might help you guys out!
When I first got into volleyball, it was because I’d seen one of my friends jump serve at a casual game we were playing. I honestly thought it was the coolest thing in the world and obsessed over it for a month, digging up any tutorials I could find, pestering everyone in my life who knew how to do it to teach me, and practicing like crazy every day. However, after weeks and weeks of hard work, I just couldn’t seem to get it...
What I’m trying to say is that I get it. Jump serves are really cool; I still think that. However, I learned the hard way that there are some prerequisite skills you should probably master before you start trying to learn how to jump serve.
Now, I’m sure you’ve probably heard that before. The whole, “you shouldn’t start jump serving yet” speech, but hear me out. I have no doubt that you could probably learn to hit a jump serve with enough determination. If your goal isn’t to use it in a competitive volleyball environment (as in you just want a cool skill to mess around with), this approach is acceptable and you can probably stop reading here. The serve’ll eventually get to a point where it’ll go over the net and maybe even look super cool, but without the basics mastered, it won’t be a good serve.
A lot of players I’ve taught start with the goal of getting serves over the net consistently. That’s a great goal to start with, but I feel that too many people make this their end goal. Think about this for a second: why did volleyball serves evolve from underhand, to overhand, to jump serves?
Because it looks way cooler!
True, but there are other aspects behind this. Power for one, but also more nuanced advantages such as control over spin and accuracy.
If you just want to make sure your serves consistently go over the net, just learn how to underhand serve. I’d go as far as to argue that underhand serves can be quite competitive, especially at lower levels of play. Skyballs are always decently effective, and it’s fairly easy to get underhand serves to float and move around. Furthermore, the fundamental mechanics of an underhand serve are extremely simple. It’ll be relatively easy to learn and master.
Now, if you’ve read that and realized serving over the net isn’t enough, you’re getting on the right track! Keep this in mind though: you still need to CONSISTENTLY serve over the net and in the court; it’s just not an end goal anymore. It doesn’t matter if you have a 70 MPH jump serve if you miss 75% of them, right?
Similarly, don’t serve to just get the ball in play. When I serve, I serve to ace. That is my sole goal. I know that sounds obvious, but really make that a concrete goal. Stop settling for just getting the ball in. Again, it’s expected you do, just make it a goal to take it further!
Now, you’re ready to start on your journey learning how to effectively jump serve! It’s time to choose which style you’d like to learn:
The Topspin Jump Serve: these serves are typically faster than floats. They have a downward spin (or topspin, hence the name) which causes the ball to move towards the ground slightly faster. This is the serve typically referred to as the “jump serve”.
The Jump Float Serve: these serves aren’t usually quite as fast or flashy, but are typically a more effective serve in game. The ball is hit with no spin, which causes it to move around mid-air. This makes it usually more difficult to pass
Almost everyone I’ve talked to finds it easier to pass a good jump serve rather than a good jump float, however, exceptional jump serves can be more effective at high levels of the sport. For this reason, I would recommend starting with the float (I did this as well); remember you can always learn the other serve later on!
Now that you’ve chosen your serve, the basic process for learning the serve is pretty similar between topspin and float.
* Start with the standing version of the serve! It’s extremely important that you learn how to hit good topspin/floats and it’s unnecessarily difficult to try to do this jumping. You have enough other things to worry about. Instead, take some time and get really good at hitting the standing versions of these serves. Consistency is key!
Also, when first learning these serves, I highly recommend focusing on getting the correct spin on the ball rather than getting it over. What I mean by that is having a serve that consistently floats but goes into the net is significantly better than a serve that goes over but never floats. The first scenario is just a matter of adjusting your aim upwards a bit as opposed to having to learn how to float.
* After you have MASTERED your standing serve, there are two more skills to master before you should start tackling your jump serve. The first is your approach and the second is your toss.
* Practice your approach without a ball. Learn all the steps and the jump. Become extremely comfortable with this to the point that you could do it in your sleep. Once this is done, combine it with the swinging mechanics you learned from your standing serve. It'll feel silly to swing at empty air over and over again, but trust me, there's no point hitting a ball if you can't do it with the proper technique. It'll just build bad habits and make it significantly more difficult for you in the future.
* Once your approach is solid, practice just tossing the ball. Again, I know it sounds stupid and like a waste of time, but it is near IMPOSSIBLE to hit a good serve with an inconsistent toss. Go through your approach, toss the ball as if you’re going to serve, and catch it at the point you plan to hit the ball. Again, you should be able to do this in your sleep before you move on to the next step.
* You’re there! It’s time to learn the jump serve! Put the approach and toss together. It may take a few reps, but the process of combining the two should be fairly straight forward.
Now, you can hit your serve, probably with considerable power. What next? Start with adjusting the trajectory of the ball. You want your ball to pass just a foot or two over the net every time you serve. This will not only give your opponents less time to watch and pass the ball, but it'll allow you to hit harder since the ball will have a better chance of staying in the court.
Finally, start training your aim. Be able to pinpoint any spot on the court and serve directly at it. I think this just comes with lots of repetition.
Here are a few more tips for maximizing the effectiveness of your serves AFTER you've learned to hit them consistently.
* When you're in game, watch for weaker passers. This seems obvious, but really pay attention to who you want to serve next.
* Aim at lines on the court (side, back). This leaves the opponents less room for error.
* Aim at the seam between two players, especially if they're weaker passers that you've identified.
I know all of these sound pretty obvious, but they do really help when serving.
This is by no means a comprehensive guide on how to learn to serve. There are a plethora of videos on the internet that do a fantastic job of that (I'd recommend the "How to SERVE a volleyball" series from Elevate Yourself). This was meant more to provide insight and advice on how to proceed about learning to serve and the mentality that should come with it.
I hope that this helped you in some way. I'm by no means perfect and still have a lot to improve on, so I'd appreciate any comments or feedback. Furthermore, if you've got any questions, I'd be happy to answer them!

"Hey guys I'm new to volleyball, I was wondering if you could help me with my jump topspin serve?" "Hey guys I've only played for 6 months but every time I try to jump serve I can't seem to get it over but I can get my standing serve over 63.27% of the time, what's wrong?" etc. etc.
Whilst I appreciate and accept that people like to learn new things and that jump serving is a pretty cool aspect of the game, the number of times I've seen new players try to jump serve, get frustrated when they can't do it very well, proceed to ask for help and someone has to explain that it's not wise to try to learn the jump serve too soon is staggering.
As such I thought I would compile the best reasons and explanations I can think of at the moment in the rest of this post for people to link to but please feel free to list your own reasonings and experience in the comments!
1. Jump serving is a very involved movement
Jump serving is a skill that combines some of the most complex and easy-to-mess-up skills of the game. You must first toss the ball to an accurate and consistent height and distance, then you must do your approach from behind the ball without running under it, then you have to broad jump and swing at a high contact point with enough force to send the ball over the net whilst maintaining good awareness of the opposite court and the accuracy to pinpoint to any seam or gap you choose. If any of these skills are lacking, the serve will fail or won't be very difficult to receive, and even worse could have a negative impact on the rest of your skills as you try to compensate which could lead to injury or bad habits. For example if someone tosses too far left when hitting right handed on a jump topspin serve, they'll have to either compensate with their approach and risk leg injury or compromise their swing and risk their shoulder.
2. You'll develop bad habits in your spiking
With such a high skill density, the jump serve is not a safe place to learn the fundamental skills required to pull it off. The swing should be practiced on it's own, as should the approach, as should the toss. By the time you get to the toss, you should have hit so many balls and done your 3 step approach so many times that you could do them perfectly on 0 hours of sleep after a 12 hour shift. If this is not the case, any bad habits that form in your swing and approach that aren't corrected immediately will transfer to your spiking, since you are essentially trying to learn how to spike at the same time as you're serving. Once you have a bad habit, it's very difficult to get out of it so it's best to take learning complex skills one step at a time.
3. The standing serve is the perfect eco-system for learning how to swing
Yes you are still tossing the ball, but not very high and the ability to shift your feet easily to adjust for a bad toss means that a standing serve is basically all about your swing. If you can't get the ball over 100% of the time and get the ball to where you're aiming like 90% of the time on a standing float, you still need to practice your standing floats. Same goes for a standing topspin but there's less use for that serve in actual play, I would recommend learning it though if only to learn the difference in follow-through and hand position required between floating and topspin serves. And as an aside, yes you need to be able to aim your float serve before you move on if you can't aim it all that tells me is you don't actually have full control over your armswing yet, the best you can do is swing and pray, and that's far from the level of mastery required to move on.
4. Jump topspin serves aren't even good unless you can hit it hard and accurate
Jump topspin serves are used in high level play as essentially a trade-off; they accept that they'll have a slightly higher serve error percentage but in turn they can throw off and intimidate the opponent with extremely fast and hard driven balls. The key here is that they are getting power in return for consistency, but if you have no power to begin with, the jump topspin is a terrible serve. Float serves on the other hand are super consistent, whilst being harder to receive despite lower ball velocities thanks to the unpredictable floating properties of the ball. So in a game setting, a pin-point standing float will get ace after ace after ace. That's not to say that a jump float doesn't have significant advantages though, but it will be a much smoother transition to the jump float if your standing float is already close to perfect.
tl;dr learn standing float -> jump float ->-> jump float hybrid ->->-> mayyyybe jump topspin
Again feel free to add more in the comments if I've missed anything. Thanks for coming to my Ted Talk, hope I helped!

After three weeks and way too many games of volleyball, the men’s world championships are over. Lots of amazing volleyball was played, many highlights made the rounds on Instagram, and most Bulgarians stayed home for matches. As for the results, Drake put it best: “Back-to-back like I’m Jordan ’96 ’97 whoa”. Congratulations to Poland for an impressive two world championships gold medals in a row. And to Brazil for the silver, the USA for the bronze, and to the rest for trying their best. We get the women’s tournament back-to-back as well! My team is almost out of it 3 days into the tournament though. Alas, because I haven’t scratched my writing itch in a while, here is ~1500 words on what this Canadian thought of the 2018 men’s edition of the tournament.
1. Unfortunately, my first thought is going to be negative. And if you have followed my podcast or videos, you probably know what it is going to be. The tournament format. This is something that is not hard to get right. For most sporting events, the structure is barely a blip on the radar of things to complain about. But the World Championships was severely hampered by strange, complicated, and frustrating decisions about how teams advance.
• The initial pools were based on horribly outdated team rankings, making the first group stage imbalanced. Poland, our eventual champions, and Italy coasted through an easy first group while France, Canada, and Brazil had a brutal initial stage to deal with. This issue was compounded by the fact that points carried over from these uneven 1st groups in the second stage. France beat our gold medalists relatively convincingly in the second round and didn’t advance to the final 6!
• The final 6. No matter what you think of the other format complaints, this is something everyone wants to get rid of. Because this out third round of pool play, we had meaningless games two days before the tournament finals. TWO DAYS. The Brazil and USA benches played each other, and Serbia didn’t care against Poland on a forgettable Friday. This is when the tension of the tournament should be ramping up, not sputtering out. Get rid of the final 6 that no other sport uses for a good reason, and at least implement an 8-team single elimination bracket.
• Too many matches. This one is more for the players, who must endure a grueling gauntlet of volleyball right before the start of their club seasons. With 12 games in such a short period, injury risk increases, and exhaustion becomes a factor. Teams really started to lose steam by the final 6, lowering the quality of play. Even as a die-hard fan it is impossible to watch every game I wanted to. Lowering the number of matches in the tournament would be a benefit to both fans and players.
2. Kurek is a beast. Holy crap that was an impressive performance in the final round. 20/29 attacking in the championship game is one of the most impressive performances of all time in a World Championship final. Almost unprecedented for a guy who we weren’t even sure was going to start at the beginning of the tournament. Just an amazing redemption story.
After being left off the gold medal team in 2014, then mailing in several disappointing club seasons, it was easy to write him off as a gifted athlete whose attitude would always hold them back. Seriously, for anyone who watched him in Ziraat Bankasi Ankara last year, he looked like he was ready to quit volleyball. Kurek’s World Championship MVP must be incredibly validating for him and I hope we get to see this Bartosz Kurek more often.
3. The production of the event could be so, so much better. Where are the pre and post-game shows? Where are announcers who know what they are talking about? Where is the analysis that goes beyond basic post-game recaps? Especially now that we are paying $20 to watch the tournament. Watching volleyball for the love of the game is great, but so much of what makes sports entertaining are the storylines that surround the players and teams. Just going from what the broadcast and website provided, you would have no context behind anything that happened in the tournament.
4. The level of volleyball in this tournament was amazingly high. We are watching the best generation of volleyball players ever, and they are only getting better. I don’t want to disrespect the players who laid the foundation for the modern game, but watching video from the 1972 Olympic Games, it barely looks like the same sport. Even the progress since the early 2000s has been astounding. There is still a lot of room left to grow in terms of both skills, athleticism, and tactics, but you are guaranteed at least one mind-blowing play every set. The fact that the quality of play on the court is so high makes all my complaints about format and production even more frustrating.
5. I already touched on this, but it deserves its own bullet point. We need better announcers! This isn’t golf, we shouldn’t have a British dude making 1-2 comments per minute about what they see in front of them. Look at big conference women’s NCAA games to see how much more enjoyable watching volleyball is when you have a knowledgeable and engaging 2-person commentary booth. Especially when you have so much downtime between timeouts, challenges, and missed serves. There are so many people who would be awesome in the booth and really improve the viewing experience.
6. There is no way I would have thought we would be having a Brazil vs Poland championship game rematch. Any final that didn’t involve one of the USA, France, or Russia seemed unlikely at the start of the tournament. Brazil was missing both its starting outside hitters in Ricardo Lucarelli and Mauricio Borges, and Poland had suffered many disappointments in the international stage since their 2014 world championship win.
But I think it's awesome that it is so hard to make predictions. We’re spoiled with contenders at the men’s senior level. Brazil, Canada, France, Italy, Poland, Russia, Serbia, and the USA all could have won medals had a couple of balls gone a different way. I’m sure we’ll see different medalists at next summer’s VNL and World Cup.
7. Following the game threads on reddit was one of my favourite volleyball-watching experiences in a while. Especially in the final round when we got contributions from a wide variety of fans. We’ve seen the concept become extremely successful for the NBA, NFL, and NHL so it makes sense that it works well for a sport with lots of breaks like volleyball. I think reddit, in general, is the best second-screen experience in sports, and I hope the game threads continue for the women’s world championships and this year’s club season.
8. Volleyball is still in the stone age when it comes to stats. We are just approaching the conclusion that most sports leagues arrived at in the 90s, which is that numbers tell us a lot about the game. The only mention of stats by the FIVB broadcast or website is when point, block, or ace records are close to being broken. I want to know if Filippo Lanza forcing opponents into poor passing situations with his serve. I want to know what outsides are hitting against Sharone Vernon-Evans in single block situations. I want to know the % difference between Taylor Sander and Aaron Russell as pipe hitters. This is a lot to ask, but it shouldn’t be. But for now, can we please get stats as per set in addition to totals.
9. I swear wipes go off the attacking player’s hand last half the time, but I have yet to see it called in the defense’s favour. This move was a point of emphasis by the FIVB but is still officiated inconsistently in my opinion.
10. If you liked watching this tournament but are sad that volleyball is over until next summer, you are in luck! The pro season is about to start, and the Italian League is looking more stacked than ever. There is also the Champions League, Russian League, Polish League, and Brazilian League with many high-level players and teams. Pick one team and become a fan! In many ways, I prefer watching the club season to international play. The slower pace makes it easier to follow and storylines develop more organically over the course of 8 months. I’ll be releasing a guide on how to follow and watch pro volleyball this season sometime next week. And maybe be doing a fantasy volleyball league so if you are interested in that let me know.
